'''Theodore E. Madey''' (October 24, 1937 – July 27, 2008) was an American [[condensed matter physicist]] who specialized in the [[chemistry]] and [[physics]] of surfaces. He was a professor in the physics and chemistry departments at [[Rutgers University]] at the time of his death.{{r|Rutgers}}

==Early life and education==
Theodore Eugene Madey was born in [[Wilmington, DE]], and was raised in [[Baltimore, MD]].{{r|Obit1}}{{r|memorial}}{{r|AVSinterview}}  He was the descendant of [[Polish American]] immigrants who were amongst a wave of immigrants that fled instability and famine in Poland at the [[turn of the century]].{{r|1940Census}} His grandparents and parents lived in Delaware's [[New Castle County, DE|New Castle County]] at the time of his birth, where his Polish-born grandfather  worked for a shipbuilding company.{{r|draftcard}} At a young age, his family relocated to [[Baltimore, MD]] where he was raised,{{r|Obit1}}{{r|memorial}}{{r|AVSinterview}} and attended [[Loyola Blakefield]] High School. {{r|memorial}} He majored in physics at [[Loyola University Maryland|Loyola College]], also in Baltimore, and completed a [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] in 1959. In the summer following his graduation he was hired by one his college professors, a graduate of the [[University of Notre Dame]], to work in a physics laboratory with vacuum materials.{{r|AVSinterview}} Madey went on to attend graduate school in physics at the [[University of Notre Dame]] and continued to work in the field of [[Vacuum engineering|vacuum science]]. He completed his Ph.D. in physics in the experimental [[condensed matter]] group of Edward Coomes in 1963.{{r|AVSinterview}}<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://academictree.org/physics/peopleinfo.php?pid=80667|title=Edward Arthur Coomes|access-date=2020-09-11}}</ref><ref>{{cite news

==Career==
Madey's first appointment after graduation was at the [[National Bureau of Standards]] (NBS), as a National Research Council post-doctoral fellow.{{r|memorial}}{{r|AVSinterview}} He was hired permanently, and remained there for 25 years, becoming the leader of the Surface Science and Kinetics group. While employed at NBS, he developed a close working relationship with [[John Yates (chemist)|John T. Yates, Jr.]], with whom he would go on to co-author more than 60 publications, and was jointly awarded the 1978 [[Samuel Wesley Stratton Award]].{{r|YatesMadey}} In 1988, he relocated to [[New Jersey]], where he was appointed as the State of New Jersey Professor of Surface Science at [[Rutgers University]], and mentored dozens of students and post-doctoral research associates.{{r|Obit1}}{{r|memorial}} He remained in this position until his death in 2008.{{r|Rutgers}} While at Rutgers, he hosted one of his former post-doctoral research associates, [[Ulrike Diebold]], and her research group into his own research laboratory when Diebold's group was forced to temporarily evacuate in 2005 from [[Tulane University]] in [[New Orleans]] because of [[Hurricane Katrina]].<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Tales from Tulane: Professors Ulrike Diebold and Larry Byers are anxious to get their labs running again|last=Wilson|first=Elizabeth|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|volume=83|pages=15–16|issue=47|date=2005-11-21|doi=10.1021/cen-v083n047.p015}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Feder|first1=Toni|journal=Physics Today|volume=58|year=2005|doi=10.1063/1.2155745|title=Science Community Rallies to Aid Students and Researchers Displaced by Hurricane Katrina|issue=11|pages=22–23|bibcode=2005PhT....58k..22F|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Madey served on a number of scientific editorial boards, and also held a variety of elected and appointed leadership roles in the [[American Vacuum Society|AVS]].{{r|memorial}}, including President (2001).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.avs.org/About/Governance/Presidents|title=AVS Presidents|access-date=2020-09-14}}</ref>  He was also extensively involved with international outreach and served as the President (1992-1995), and Secretary-General (1986-1989) of the [[International Union for Vacuum Science, Technique and Applications]] (IUVSTA).{{r|AVSinterview}}

==Research ==
Madey's research activities fell into three areas:{{r|memorial}}{{r|homepage}}

*"Surface structure, [[Electronics|electronic]] properties, and [[Reactivity (chemistry)|reactivity]] of [[Alloy|bimetallic]] surfaces by [[atom]]ic-resolution [[scanning tunneling microscopy]], [[electron diffraction]], and [[synchrotron radiation]].
*Mechanisms of [[electron]] - and [[photon]]-stimulated [[desorption]] of atoms and ions from surfaces (including charge transfer and energy transfer phenomena) using unique apparatus that  permits angle-resolved ion detection.
*[[Nucleation]], growth, [[epitaxial]] structure and interfacial reactivity of ultrathin metal films on  [[oxide]] surfaces and on [[polymer]] surfaces using electron and ion [[spectroscopy|spectroscopies]], coupled with high resolution (sub-nanometer) electron microscopy."

His technique using [[desorption]] of atoms induced by electronic transitions to study surfaces was known as (DIET).{{r|DIET}} It involved striking a surface with [[photons]] or [[electrons]] so as to cause an [[adsorbate]] to transition into a repulsive [[excited state]], which if long-lived enough would cause it to be ejected from the surface carrying a significant amount of energy. In the case of a dielectric sample such as a [[halide]] or [[oxide]], the phenomenon is capable of causing the ejection of surface atoms, leading to electron- or photon beam damage in surface analytical methods such as [[Auger Electron Spectroscopy]] or [[Photoelectron]] Spectroscopy. It also provided an explanation for why the atmosphere of the Moon and of Mercury  have atmospheres enriched in sodium and potassium because of their exposure to [[solar wind]].<ref>{{Cite journal| first1=B.V.|last1=Yakshinskiy|first2=T.E.|last2=Madey|title= Photon-stimulated desorption as a substantial source of sodium in the lunar atmosphere|journal=Nature|volume=400|year=1999|issue=6745|pages=642–644|doi=10.1038/23204|pmid=10458159|bibcode=1999Natur.400..642Y|s2cid=4303038}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/1999/08/990809121137.htm|title=Rutgers Researchers Recreate The Moon's Atmosphere In The Lab|access-date=2020-09-14}}</ref> In collaboration with [[John Yates (chemist)|John T. Yates, Jr.]], Madey studied abrasion of [[monumental brass]] in historical structures. Their work is credited with playing a significant role in allowing the rubbing of brass to continue as a cleaning method, by revealing a rubbing method for brass that cleaned without abrading or destroying it.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Yates|first1=J.|last2=Madey|first2=T.E.|last3=Rook|first3=H.|title=Wear of English Monumental Brasses caused by Brass Rubbing|journal=Nature|volume=243|pages=422–424|year=1973|issue=5407|doi=10.1038/243422a0|bibcode=1973Natur.243..422Y|s2cid=4186139}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.buildingconservation.com/articles/monumentalbrasses/monumental-brasses.htm|title=Monumental brasses|access-date=2020-09-14}}</ref>
Madey also co-authored, along with [[Patricia Thiel]], a highly cited and comprehensive review article describing the interactions and properties of water near solid surfaces.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Thiel|first1=Patricia A.|last2=Madey|first2=Theodore E.|title=The interaction of water with solid surfaces: Fundamental aspects|journal=Surface Science Reports|volume=7|issue=6–8|year=1987|pages=211–385|issn=0167-5729|doi=10.1016/0167-5729(87)90001-X|bibcode=1987SurSR...7..211T}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hodgson|first1=A.|last2=Haq|first2=S.|year=2009|title=Water adsorption and the wetting of metal surfaces|journal = Surface Science Reports|language=en|volume=64|issue=9|pages=381–451|doi=10.1016/j.surfrep.2009.07.001|bibcode=2009SurSR..64..381H}}</ref>

A special issue of the ''[[Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter]]'' was published in 2010 to honor his memory.{{r|DIET}}

==Honors and awards==
Madey received numerous awards and honors for the quality and creativity of his work, including an honorary [[Doctorate Honoris Causa]] from the [[University of Wroclaw]] in [[Poland]] in 2004, in recognition of a decade-long collaboration with colleagues in Poland.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://uni.wroc.pl/o-uniwersytecie/nagrody-i-wyroznienia__trashed/doktorzy-honoris-causa/|title=Doktorzy honoris causa Uniwersytetu Wrocławskiego|access-date=2020-09-19}}</ref>
Other honors include:
* 1971 Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1971&unit_id=&institution=|title=APS Fellows archive|access-date=2020-09-14}}</ref>
* 1978 [[Samuel Wesley Stratton Award]], jointly with John T. Yates, "for an unusually significant research contribution to science or engineering that merits the acclaim of the scientific world and supports [[NIST]]'s mission objectives"{{r|YatesMadey}}  
* 1993 Fellow of the [[American Vacuum Society]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.avs.org/Awards-Recognition/Society-Honors/Fellow-of-the-Society|title=AVS Fellows|access-date=2020-09-04}}</ref>
* 1985 [[Medard W. Welch Award]],"For his investigations of surface processes at a fundamental atomic and molecular level, especially the determination of absorbed molecule bonding geometries."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.avs.org/Awards-Recognition/Professional-Awards/Medard-W-Welch-Award|access-date=2020-09-14|title=AVS Professional awards: Medard W. Welch Award}}</ref>
* 2003 Inducted into the [[NIST]] Gallery of Distinguished Scientists<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nist.gov/system/files/documents/2019/10/07/portrait_gallery_program_brochure_2019.pdf|title=NIST Gallery of Distinguished Scientists, Engineers, and Administrators - 2019|access-date=2020-09-14}}</ref>

Two years after Madey's death in 2008, the Theodore E. Madey Award was established by AVS to commemorate both his research and his leadership in international interactions of the AVS. The Award recipient is sponsored to visit Poland, present a seminar at the University, and engage in scientific discussions.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.avs.org/Awards-Recognition/Division-Group-Professional-Awards/Theodore-E-Madey-Award-for-Surface-Science-and-Sci|title=Theodore E. Madey Award for Surface Science|access-date=2020-09-14}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Madey was born on October 24, 1937, in Wilmington, Delaware. He met his wife, Jane Mary Madey (Gunn), while he was in college by gaining access to a cast party following her performance at a nearby college.{{r|JaneMaryObit}} They were married for 48 years, until his death on July 27, 2008, in Somerset, New Jersey.  They had four children, Timothy Madey, Doretta Witt, Maureen O'Shea, and Daniel Madey, the first of whom was born while Madey was in graduate school at the [[University of Notre Dame]].{{r|Obit1}}{{r|JaneMaryObit}}
